blocks.text: To the same effect is the fact that the Jews were always convinced that the eating of the ostrich had been forbidden them by the law of God, as the Greek and Chaldee versions of the law amply show, together with the constant practice of the Jews. Therefore, when Lampridius relates that Heliogabalus several times served ostriches and camels at his banquets, saying it was commanded to the Jews that they should eat them, some notable corruption certainly lurks in the last words, since they are utterly false. For where did God command the Jews to eat either camels or ostriches? On the contrary, he expressly forbids both. Concerning the camel the matter is certain. Concerning the ostrich it is also certain among the ancient Jews, not one of whom understood by בת יענה bath jaana anything other than the ostrich. Therefore those who, instead of struthiones et camelos [ostriches and camels], read from the Palatine codex, with the words joined, struthio-camelos, that is, ostriches, achieve nothing. For the prohibition of ostriches is no less explicit [col. 225] than that of camels. Yet let us grant that ostriches are not forbidden in the law: will it follow that the Jews were commanded to eat them? Who does not know how great the difference is between conceding something as permitted and commanding the same as necessary? These certainly differ as much as freedom ἀδιάφορος [adiaphoros] toward either alternative differs from necessity determined to one. But even if we also concede that the eating of ostriches was not only permitted but even commanded to the Jews, both of which are utterly false, what has this to do with Heliogabalus? Is it credible that a heathen, impious and altogether godless man had it in mind to obey the Jewish laws and to shape his conduct [II, 821] by their prescriptions? Since these things are wholly absurd, let more learned men consider whether the words of Lampridius may be read thus: He several times served ostriches and camels at his banquets, saying it was a command of his God that they should eat them. When he set camels and ostriches before his friends, since such cheap meat had little appeal to those dainty men, he pretended that it was a command of his God that they should eat them, that is, that this belonged to the religion and worship of his God, namely Heliogabalus, whose priest he was. The same Lampridius says above: Now he was a priest of Heliogabalus, that is, of Jupiter or of the Sun. And a little later: He was first called Varius, afterwards Heliogabalus, from his priesthood of the god Heliogabalus, whom he brought with him from Syria and for whom he established a temple at Rome on the spot where formerly the shrine of Orcus had stood. Likewise: He consecrated Heliogabalus on the Palatine hill beside the imperial palace and built him a temple, striving to transfer into that temple the image of the Mother, the fire of Vesta, the Palladium, the shields, and everything held sacred by the Romans, and aiming that no god but Heliogabalus should be worshipped at Rome. He said moreover that the religions of the Jews and Samaritans and the Christian devotion must be transferred there, so that the priesthood of Heliogabalus might hold the secret of every cult. And below: He carried off the image which he believed to be the Palladium, and, having had it cast in gold, placed it in the temple of his God. And again: And the sacred name, carried off, he transferred to the inner sanctuary of his God. Likewise: He declared that all the gods were ministers of his God. So here: Saying it was a command of his God that they should eat them. From the words Dei sui [of his God], or sui Dei, the ignorance of scribes seems to have made, κατ᾽ ἀναγραμματισμὸν [kat᾽ anagrammatismon], Iudaeis [to the Jews]. And after aliquoties [several times] the word esse was omitted because of τὸ ὁμοιόπτωτον [to homoioptōton]. However that may be, since the Greek, Latin, Chaldee, Syriac, Arabic and Hebrew interpreters agree in the same rendering of the word יענה jaana, I do not see that one can safely depart from all of them unless there are weighty reasons, and I see none such here. For why should not בת יענה filia jaana [daughter of jaana] be thought to be the ostrich? Let the passages of Scripture in which it is mentioned be examined: what will be found in them that does not suit the ostrich?
